snippets: Repeated, episodic bouts of skeletal muscle contraction undertaken frequently as structured exercise training are a potent stimulus for physiological adaptation in many organs. Specifically, in skeletal muscle, remarkable plasticity is demonstrated by the remodeling of muscle structure and function in terms of muscular size, force, endurance, and contractile velocity as a result of the functional demands induced by various types of exercise training.

The “mechanisms” underpinning adaptation, rather than the adaptive changes themselves that occur in skeletal muscle in response to exercise training, will be the major focus of this review. The remodeling of muscle structure and function, with respect to alterations in muscular size, force, endurance, and contractile velocity as a result of changes in functional demand induced by various types of exercise training, has been reviewed extensively elsewhere (4, 17–21).

Some of the first observations on the molecular basis of adaptations in skeletal muscle to exercise training were changes in mRNA abundance in response to various models of contractile activity (26–31) and aerobic (32) and resistance (33) exercise training. However, these studies could not definitively distinguish whether changes in mRNA abundance in response to chronic contractile activity or exercise training were the result of a new steady-state rate of transcription or a transient increase in transcription during recovery.

Together, these data suggested that transient increases in transcription during recovery from consecutive sessions of exercise resulted in a gradual accumulation of mRNA and, therefore, represented the underlying kinetic basis for the cellular adaptations associated with exercise training, i.e., enhanced abundance of gene transcripts are the information for the synthesis of protein components that provoke structural remodeling and functional adjustments in the long term (cf. Ref. 22). Within a few years, the deployment of microarrays for gene expression analysis on a broader scale (rather than the previous approaches of investigating candidate genes) revealed the large numbers of genes whose mRNA abundance was altered by acute exercise in human skeletal muscle (46, 47).
